description: Fetch the provider's root page and extract all <a href="..."> links. Look for URLs whose text or path suggests they match the target field (e.g., 'pricing', 'login', 'docs', 'api'). This is useful when the target URL is linked from the homepage.

Search the web for the provider's name combined with the field keyword. For example, if looking for a pricing page, search for '<provider name> pricing' or '<provider name> API pricing'. Use this when the URL isn't obvious from the provider's own site.

Fetch /robots.txt from the provider's domain. The Allow and Disallow directives often list paths that are relevant to the target field. Construct full URLs by combining the domain with discovered paths.

Fetch /sitemap.xml (or a sitemap index) to get a comprehensive list of all pages on the provider's site. Parse <loc> elements and match URLs against the target field keywords (pricing, login, docs, api).
If the current URL is broken and no working alternative is found, query the Wayback Machine CDX API for archived snapshots. This is a fallback for sites that have changed or gone down.
For API baseUrl fields: Many cloud providers (Alibaba, Tencent, etc.) have region-specific endpoints. If a URL returns 404, try regional variants.

Find and read the provider's official API documentation. Strategy: (1) use the provider's own documentationUrl if available; (2) search the web for '<provider name> API documentation' as fallback; (3) scan the provider's website for doc/API pages.

When the target URL returns HTTP 404 or is unreachable, research alternatives. Strategy: (1) test common sub-paths like {baseUrl}/models; (2) search the web for '<provider name> API base URL'; (3) fetch the provider's website for API endpoint examples; (4) try common API paths.

Before accepting a baseUrl as correct, validate it behaves like a real API endpoint. Strategy: (1) check that the URL returns a valid HTTP response; (2) test {baseUrl}/models or other documented paths; (3) verify the response body is valid JSON; (4) HTTP 401 with JSON body counts as valid.

Research the provider's documentation to determine if they expose an endpoint to list available models. Look for endpoints like GET /v1/models, GET /api/tags, 'list models', or similar model listing endpoints.

Research the correct public website URL for this provider — the website MUST be publicly accessible (HTTP 200-399). Prefer root domains over subdomains. NEVER suggest a URL whose domain has no relationship to the provider name.

Research the correct login/sign-in page URL for this provider. Strategy: (1) fetch_url the provider's website and scan HTML for login-related <a> tags; (2) look for href containing: 'login', 'signin', 'sign-in', 'auth'; (3) search_web for '<provider name> login' as fallback.

Research the correct API documentation URL for this provider. Strategy: (1) search_web for '<provider name> API documentation'; (2) documentation is typically on docs.provider.com, developer.provider.com, or provider.com/docs; (3) fetch_url found pages and verify they contain technical API content.

Decision rule for baseUrl fields behind API-key gateways that answer 401/403 with non-JSON bodies on every path (e.g. DeepSeek), so Base URL Validation's JSON check can never pass anonymously. Applies only after that JSON check fails. Decision steps: (1) extract endpoint paths documented on the same host from the pre-fetched official documentation; (2) ACCEPT if any documented endpoint returns a JSON body (JSON error bodies count); (3) otherwise ACCEPT only if documented endpoints answer with 401/403 auth challenges AND the documentation explicitly names this host as the API base URL (base_url/baseURL assignment in tables or SDK samples); (4) REJECT in all other cases — a bare 401 alone never passes.

Use declarative JSON decision trees (loaded from Config/trees/) instead of the step-by-step micro-prompt workflow for URL research. When enabled, the DecisionTreeResearchService replaces AutonomousUrlResearchAgent as the IUrlResearchService implementation.
